Canadian Camping 





EDITORIAL 


WHAT A CAMPER 
EXPECTS FROM 
CAMP 

Camp has a tremendous appeal to 
youth and it is apparent that some of 
us in camping have taken advantage of 
this fact to lure children to a so-called 
camp setting, which is a far cry from 
that envisioned by the camper. Such 
institutions are, in some cases, little 
more than baby sitting agencies or 
glorified summer resorts. 

What does the word “camp” mean 
to a youngster? Camp should mean 
adventure and excitement, but surelv 
it suggests something more—a life com¬ 
pletely different from that of the city. 
Canada as a relatively young frontier 
country, has a wealth of fabled and real 
figures who themselves were campers 
in the true sense of the word. Our 
children today study in history, or 
watch on TV, such characters as Hia¬ 
watha, Paul Bunyan, Davey Crockett, 
Daniel Boone and Radisson. It is there¬ 
fore not surprising that they conjure up 
a picture of adventurous outdoor living 
in attempting to re-create the role of 
their hero. 

Children have some pretty exciting 
pre-conceived ideas of what camp 
should be like. We need to look a little 
more closely at the camp and its pro¬ 
gram through the youngster’s eyes. If 
we do, some of the following character¬ 
istics should emerge as important. 


by Robert E. Wilkinson, 

Assistant Professor of Physical Education, 
McGill University, and 

Director, Junior Gamp, Camp Nominingue. 


CAMP IS FUN. 

In what way does the child expect 
camp to be fun? The answer lies surely 
in an environment which is “campy”, 
which provides the opportunity of 
learning skills which are indigenous to 
camp and outdoor living. To deprive a 
child of the opportunity to sleep in a 
tent, to build his own fire, and to cook 
a meal over this fire, is to deprive him 
of the basic ingredients that make up 
the camp setting. 

There will always be parents who 
will question the value of these experi¬ 
ences, on the basis that “there is no 
place in our modern urban society for 
such out-moded skills as canoeing, 
woodcraft and axemanship in an age of 
motorboats, electric stoves and gas 
ranges”. An answer to this group is 
that one of the main objectives of 
modern camping should be education 
for leisure time. This places increasing 
demands on the individual to develop 
self-directed activities for leisure time 
use. The camp can play a vital role in 
supplying such carry-over skills as fish¬ 
ing, hunting, hiking and canoeing. 
They must, however, be so pleasing and 
satisfying to the youngster that he will 
continue to pursue these forms of rec¬ 
reation long after his camp days are 
over. 


Toronto, Canada, April 1961 


99 





Family camping is growing by leaps 
and bounds all over the country, and 
although provincial governments un¬ 
fortunately have been slow to recog¬ 
nize this trend, some provinces are now 
providing State Park facilities to ac¬ 
commodate this great movement of 
Canadian families to the out-of-doors. 

If we accept that these basic camp 
experiences are important, we should 
probably go further and re-direct our 
emphasis in program planning toward 
such skills as swimming, canoeing, arch¬ 
ery, orienteering and axemanship, ra¬ 
ther than the promotion of school and 
playground activities like football, base¬ 
ball and basketball. The camp program 
should be essentially unique, it should 
complement, not duplicate, activities 
already learned before coming to camp. 

Another important value of the learn¬ 
ing of these camp skills is the knowl¬ 
edge they give for survival. After al¬ 
most any week-end we can read in our 
local papers of Canadians who perished 
in our out-of-doors or drowned in our 
rivers and lakes. It is reasonable to 
assume that nearly all of these persons 
could have survived with the knowledge 
that the young camper should learn at 
camp. 

A further argument in defense of the 
inclusion of the real camp skills is the 
fact that much can be done to educate 
our youth to a deeper appreciation and 
understanding of the great outdoors. 
To give but one example—surely the 
product of a good camp experience will 
have a real appreciation of the impor¬ 
tance of reforestation and conservation 
of our natural resources. 

These then are the skills and activi¬ 
ties that the child really expects at 
camp. They are neither difficult nor 
expensive to provide. 

CAMP MEANS FREEDOM 

The camper of today expects freedom 


at camp—a good measure of freedom— 
more than he receives at school, and 
more than most youngsters experience 
at home. Freedom should not be con¬ 
fused with anarchy. There are numer¬ 
ous studies to show that children look 
for and respect firm but fair leadership. 
They are looking for the same freedom 
that you and I would want for our¬ 
selves, and this implies a respect for 
the rights and feelings of others. Speci¬ 
fically, the youngster is looking for 
freedom from worry and anxiety; free¬ 
dom from over-strain; freedom to 
choose activities and programs; free¬ 
dom to have a part in program plan¬ 
ning; freedom to follow his own indi¬ 
vidual interests in time that is not pre¬ 
planned for him. 

Too often we have tended to go 
overboard in this concept of the 
“camper centred program”, where the 
youngster is given complete freedom to 
choose and plan his own program. If 
this is our approach to programming, 
it seems difficult to justify the need for 
senior program directors who have 
years of training and experience de¬ 
signed to plan the best possible pro¬ 
gram for children. Certainly we should 
encourage the camper to express his 
“interests ” but it is very doubtful 
whether the camper is the best person 
to determine his own needs. The camo 
that takes cognizance of the camper’s 
interests and allows the camper to make 
choices and judgments under firm but 
sympathetic leadership, is the camn 
that provides a camper’s type of 
freedom. 

CAMP PROVIDES 
COMRADESHIP 

Camp provides the ideal laboratory 
for children to learn to live and work 
together — to learn how to establish 
satisfactory relationships with one’s 
fellows. Through the small cabin or 
tent group, the camper finds out that 


100 


Canadi\n Camping 




this business of living is chiefly a matter leisurely and personal. Let us never 

of getting along with others. What allow our camps to become so organized 

better place to learn the lessons of un- and efficient as to reduce the personal 

selfishness, fair play, cooperation and contact between camper and staff mem- 

respect for the feelings of others than ber, which is so fundamental to the 

at camp. growth of the child. 


One of the best ways that we can 
teach some of these lessons in group 
living is through shared camp projects. 
This does not refer to daily menial 
chores, or “joe” jobs, but rather larger 
staff-directed projects which contribute 
to camp improvement. Such projects, 
when staff supported, result in the 
campers taking an interest and pride in 
his camp which he never felt before. 
Many parents have related that the 
highlight of the camp season for their 
boy was the feeling of pride derived 
from assisting in the construction of an 
outdoor chapel, or some similar pro¬ 
ject, because, for this boy, it gave real 
meaning and purpose to the whole 
summer. 

The comradeship that the camper is 
asking us to provide is not only fellow¬ 
ship with other campers, but also with 
staff. There is no question that good 
leadership is the real key to the success¬ 
ful camp experience. What are the 
characteristics of a good leader or coun¬ 
sellor? Again, if we approach the prob¬ 
lem through the mind of the camper, 
three questions will head the list: Does 
he have a sincere interest in, and lik¬ 
ing, for us? Is he full of fun and does 
he have plenty of energy and enthusi¬ 
asm? Does he have a love for, and 
knowledge of camp skills? 

Comradeship between staff and cam¬ 
per depends very largely on the over-all 
size of the camp. Large, successful 
camps, must recognize the danger of 
jeopardizing this personal fellowship 
between staff member and camper by 
organizing and regimenting many rou¬ 
tines which used to be much more 


CAMP DEVELOPS A LOVE 
OF NATURE. 

The final basic need of the camper 
is the development of an appreciation 
of and respect for nature. Some might 
term this the spiritual food of the camp 
experience. Almost every young child 
has an innate, insatiable curiosity in 
nature’s wonders, and it is only over a 
period of years that we manage to stul¬ 
tify this curiosity so that by his teens 
the child has developed a hard-shelled 
attitude, where to show an interest in 
nature and its wonders is to be labelled 
a sissy. Here again, leadership is im¬ 
portant. The sympathetic staff member 
can nurture this natural interest and 
ciriosity. 

Albert Swcitzer has said: “The most 
important years in life are those be¬ 
tween 9 and 14. This is the time to ac¬ 
quaint the young with the great spirit¬ 
ual values of mankind—afterwards it 
is too late”. Camp has an unique op¬ 
portunity to provide every camper with 
an increased understanding and appre¬ 
ciation of God’s great outdoors. Who 
has not been moved by a beautiful sun¬ 
set, a spider’s web in the early morning 
dew or the cry of the loon at dusk? 
These are unforgettable “spiritual 
moments”. 

We must, however, be careful to 
realize that we cannot lecture children 
on the beauty of such experiences. 
Rather, we attempt to develop and 
deepen their appreciation with a much 
more subtle approach. This means ex- 

turn to page 127 


Toronto, Canada , April 1961 


101 



m n 

^ot'JMHieSterS 

& ^tnsfjtp of OTooDgmen 

Kirk A, W. Wipper 
Camp Kandalore 


It is inevitable that people who 
undertake to explore the natural world 
around find a bond with others who 
have also learned of peace and happi¬ 
ness through such a pursuit. To this 
mutual interest must be attributed the 
formation of the “Norwesters* ” organ¬ 
ization. This group of young men, all 
camp staff members, are proficient in 
skills of tripping, exploration, orienteer¬ 
ing, canoeing, campcraft, woodlore, 
wildlife and creative crafts using natur¬ 
al materials. Their purpose is to pro¬ 
mote, practice, and teach other camp¬ 
ers these skills, all of which are related 
to the natural environment. This pur¬ 
pose is based on their belief that the 
essence of real camping must be in a 
deliberate and conscientious identifica¬ 
tion with their surroundings. To ac¬ 
complish this purpose, the Norwesters 
are, of course, most active through the 
camping season but, in addition, meet 
throughout the off camp season. 

During the summer, the Norwesters 
are heads of various activities in 
which they are particularly skilled. The 
tripping staff, the canoe head, the 
campcraft specialists, the wildlife direc¬ 
tor, the arts and crafts director, and 
some of the section directors and senior 


counsellors are members of this organi¬ 
zation. Their influence on the direc¬ 
tion and purpose of the camp is power¬ 
ful indeed. One of the advantages of 
this kind of interest group is that a 
great deal of co-operation between 
activities is achieved. For example, it 
is not unusual for arts and crafts, 
campcraft and wildlife specialists to 
work together in the construction of a 
genuine Huron shelter—an example of 
a project designed to acquaint campers 
with the techniques of early Canadian 
History. There is adventure in dis¬ 
covering something of the wilderness 
wisdom of the past. 

In addition, the Norwesters present 
special events such as a campfire in 
which useful and interesting camping 
techniques are demonstrated. The pre¬ 
paration of wintergreen tea, the plank¬ 
ing and roasting of fresh fish, the meth¬ 
ods of making various natural foods 
palatable, boiling water in a birch bark 
container, or starting fires without 
matches are but a few of the items 
chosen by this group for such occasions. 
Through an event of this kind, the Nor¬ 
westers can directly challenge campers 
toward better camping technique. 


102 


Canadian Camping 




To further develop their own skills 
the Nor westers conduct major projects 
of their own as well. For example, the 
members of this group have carried out 
extensive trips into most of the Hali- 
burton, Algonquin and Temagami re¬ 
gions. Their plans will lead them to 
many other magnificent tripping areas. 
In addition, two of their members suc¬ 
cessfully carried through an experiment 
in survival camping in which they lived 
lor seven days in a remote location, 
with foods gleaned from the natural 
surroundings, and by fires started with¬ 
out matches. 

Membership in the Norwesters is 
gained by invitation usually after a 
candidate has revealed particular skill 
in the activities important to them. He 
must also be interested in participating 
enthusiastically in the purpose for 
which the group exists. The fellowship 


and lasting friendships gained from this 
association are a real attraction for 
prospective members. Currently, the 
Norwesters have, in the active member¬ 
ship, men who have graduated from the 
camp staff and who still retain their 
interest in promoting the group’s goals. 
This contact is invaluable. The ex¬ 
perience and skill of older members can 
reasonably benefit newer entrants to 
the Norwesters, who are actively en¬ 
gaged as camp stafT members. 

The spirit of this unique group is well 
represented in the verse they have 
chosen as their motto: 

In the strengths of our forefathers we go 
Not in their footsteps 
It is their stars we follow 
Not their dead campfires. 

— •

Toronto, Canada , April 1961

SURVIVAL 

SWIMMING 

Rodd Gleeson 

Physical Director, Regina Y.M.C.A. 


As early as the 1930’s, Fred Lanoue, 
a Professor at the Georgia Institute of 
Technology, was concerned with the 
inability of excellent swimmers to sur¬ 
vive when caught in large bodies of 
water without a means of support. Sur¬ 
vival swimming, (also known as drown 
proofing—considered by some as nega¬ 
tive terminology), is the result of many 
years of study and research on his part. 

During the war, Dr. Lanoue taught 
survival swimming to the U.S. Navy 
with the objective in mind of helping 
service men to remain afloat in the 
ocean until they could be picked up by 
rescue craft. One ex-Georgia Tech 
student visited Dr. Lanoue after the 
war and told him that he had floated 
around in the ocean for some five hours 
with both bones broken in one forearm 


and the other one badly burned. Be¬ 
cause of having learned the survival 
swimming skill, he was able to stay 
afloat until help arrived while hundreds 
of his shipmates drowned. 

What makes this method so easy? 
How can a person remain afloat for 
hours with limbs tied or broken? In 
order to stay afloat, man must have his 
nose or mouth clear of the water. 
Treading water methods have been 
developed over the years which require 
the head to be kept above water or 
arched backwards. Survival swimming 
provides a method of staying afloat 
without having to keep the weight of 
the head above the water, or to assume 
an unnatural position such as the neck 
extended backwards. 

To prove how tiring it is to tread 
water, try to keep a 10 lb. block out 
of the water while swimming on your 
back. How illogical it is then to try to 
tread with your head (15 lbs.) above 
water. Or, if you are a floater, lie back 
in the water and see how long you are 
able to float without an aching neck or 
a mouth full of water. 

Survival swimming has been designed 
to make the maximum amount of use 
of the body’s natural buoyancy. The 
average density of a human being is 
.97. This means that with lungs full 
of air, he is able to float on the surface 
in a relaxed position with approximate¬ 
ly five pounds of his body out of the 
water. Breathing is accomplished by 
exhaling below the surface, gently sur¬ 
facing, inhaling, and relaxing again. 
Survival swimming has the person as¬ 
sume a more natural and relaxed posi¬ 
tion using a minimum amount of ener-. 
gv during the exchange of air process. 
This can be maintained for many hours 
without fatigue. 

Aquatic directors who are responsible 
for the teaching of swimming should 
seriously consider using this method 


104 


Canadian Camping 



rather than the conventional and more 
widely publicized methods, as endorsed 
by the Red Cross, Y.M.C.A. and others. 
The only skill required to learn survival 
swimming is the jelly fish float. When 
this has been mastered, it is a simple 
matter to develop self confidence in the 
pupil and progress him through the 
stages of survival swimming. In addi¬ 
tion, when he masters this stroke, it is 
easy to introduce him to the side stroke. 
This type of progression emphasizes 
relaxation and slow movements of the 
arms and legs. Compare this to the 
confused individual attempting to co¬ 
ordinate arms, legs, and breathing 
required for the crawl stroke. For these 
reasons, adults find it easier to learn 
to swim using the survival method. An 
additional reason for teaching adults 
this method is that many of them want 
to swim for recreation only and the side 
stroke suffices. 

For boys and girls of camp age, it 
has been found better to teach these 
skills at an advanced level. They will 
learn very fast and it will not take 
much program time. 

The 1956 revision of the Y.M.C.A. 
swimming manual has included drown 
proofing as an alternate requirement in 
its third star program. However, many 
people choose the alternative, which is 
to tread water for thirty seconds with 
their hands in the water. Even the 
small percentage choosing drown proof¬ 
ing, need only do it for one minuate 
and this does not provide an adequate 
demonstration of the skill that has been 
acquired. 

Magazines have published reports on 
this method and to mention only a 
few: Life Magazine, June 11, 1951, 
Coronet, July 1952, and lately the 
Reader’s Digest, July 1960 issue, and 
Every Woman’s Family Circle, June 
1960. It would be worthwhile to read 
the articles of last summer. 


In children’s camping, the sponsoring 
organization or camp owner, has an 
obligation to the campers and their 
parents to teach basic survival skills as 
well as advanced swimming, ornamen¬ 
tal swimming and fancy diving. Occa¬ 
sions will arise when such a skill will 
mean the difference between life or 
death, not only while camping but in 
other phases of normal living. 

Survival swimming should be a re¬ 
quirement for boys participating in an 
out trip program at camp. It is not 
known if any camp insists upon this at 
the present time. However, survival 
swimming has been taught at some 
camps in Canada. During camp water 
shows, it is always interesting to parents 
and spectators to see several boys in a 
corner of the swimming area, some with 
their hands and legs tied with rope, 
staying afloat for the entire length of 
the swim demonstration. This impres¬ 
ses upon them the importance of having 
such a skill, and helps to reassure them 
that their child is receiving necessary 
survival instruction while at camp. 
Some camp directors will say that this 
skill would take too much program 
time, that all canoe trips, whether cros¬ 
sing a large lake or not, stick to within 
easy reach of the shore and therefore 
this skill is not necessary. However, I 
would submit that many canoe trips do 
not stick close to shore when crossing a 
lake and that sometime a disaster will 
be avoided if the participants of the 
trip have such a skill. 

Survival swimming is important in 
camping, important enough to make it 
a part of the regular swimming pro¬ 
gram along with artificial respiration 
and water safety. Camping must in¬ 
clude preventative programs which will 
provide a broad base for a more enjoy¬ 
able and safer experience. 

—• 


Toronto , Canada , April 1961

NOBODY NEEDS TO DROWN! 

Here is a sun pie scheme which anyone over four can use 
to cope confidently with the water in an emergency 

By permission of Reader's Digest — 
Joseph P . Blank 



Studies indicate that the principal 
causes of drowning are panic and ex¬ 
haustion. In panic, nonswimmers and 
even some swimmers struggle to Hold 
their heads above water, which no one 
can do for long. Soon exhausted, they 
go down. 

During the last 25 years a technique 
has been developed which can prevent 
death in the water. Aimed at freeing 
the potential drowning victim from 
hysteria and energy-draining tension, it 
is called Drownproofing. Worked out 
by Fred R. Lanoue, professor of physi¬ 
cal education and head swimming 
coach at Georgia Institute of Tech¬ 
nology, it consists of two simple 
“strokes”: the Stay-Afloat Stroke and 
the Travel Stroke. Using these. La¬ 
noue has taught 20,000 people of all 
ages—swimmers and non-swimmers— 
how to stay afloat in an emergency for 
hours, or how to travel at least a mile 
without fatigue. 

The theory behind Drown proofing is 
this: muscle and bone sink: fat and 
air float. The proportions of each in 


the human body are such that, with 
lungs fully inflated, 98 out of 100 men 
and practically all women will float 
against the surface of the water if they 
don't try to hold their heads up. 

In Drownproofing, then, you hang 
relaxed in a near-vertical position in 
the water, letting your head dangle, 
face down. Every few seconds you raise 
your head for a change of air. 

Here, in the diagrams that follow, 
are the two strokes—one to stay afloat, 
one to get to shore without tiring: 

STAY-AFLOAT STROKE 

1. Take a breath and immediately lay 
your head forward in the water until 
your chin is on your chest. Relax your 
entire body, letting your hands dangle. 
If you’re fat, you may find your but¬ 
tocks swinging upward. Exhale a little 
air through your nose and you will 
return to the vertical position. Rest, 
just “hanging” in the water. The back 
of your head will protrude slightlv 
above the surface. 


106 


Canadian Camping 





2. After a few seconds, but before you 
need air, leisurely cross your arms in 
front of your head, forearms together. 
Raise one knee toward your chest, then 
extend the foot forward. Simultaneous¬ 
ly, extend the other foot behind you. 
Move easily and smoothly so you re¬ 
main vertical, head lolling. 

3. Raise your head quickly but smooth¬ 
ly. stopping with your chin still in the 
water. As you raise your head, exhale 
through your nose, beginning while 
your face is under water and continu¬ 
ing as it emerges. 

4. Finish exhaling: open your mouth 
to inhale. To keep your mouth above 
water while you inhale, gently sweep 
your palms outward and step down¬ 
ward on the water with both feet. 
Don’t move too vigorously or you will 
pop your shoulders out of the water. 
You don’t need a 100-percent change 
of air; experiment to learn just how 
much you need. 

5. Having inhaled, close your mouth, 
drop your head toward your chest, your 
arms toward your knees. Relax, go 
limp, in the same position as in Step 1. 
If you tend to sink a few feet below the 
surface, it is because you have failed to 
drop your arms after putting your head 
in the water. When you need another 
breath, swing smoothly into Steps 2, 3, 
4 and 5 again. If your chest feels tight 
under water, either you are resting too 
long or you are not exhaling deeply 
enough. Adjust these factors through 
repeated practice. 


TRAVEL STROKE 

1. Take a breath, sink vertically. As 
your head goes under, push down gent¬ 
ly with your hands to arrest any tend¬ 
ency to sink too deep. 

2. Tip your head forward to the face¬ 
down position. Bring your hands to 
your forehead and open-scissor your 
legs with the rear foot raised as high 
as possible. This will begin to swing 
your body into a horizontal position. 

3. Extend your arms forward and to¬ 
ward the surface, hands together. The 
moment they are extended full length, 
give a scissors kick with your legs. 

4. As your feet come together from the 
kick, slowly sweep your arms outward 
and back, finishing the stroke with your 
hands at your thighs. Make the move¬ 
ment easily. 

5. As you glide forward and upward, 
keep your body relaxed and your hand*? 
at your thighs, and begin to exhale 
through your nose. 

6. When you’re ready for a fresh 
breath (don’t wait until you need it), 
begin returning to the vertical position 
by bowing your back, bringing both 
knees toward your chest and raising 
your hands toward your head. Con¬ 
tinue exhaling through this and Step 7. 

7. Continue swinging toward the ver¬ 
tical by extending one leg in front of 
you and bringing the other knee up to 
it. Cross your arms in front of your 
head, forearms together, palms out. 

turn to page 135 


Toronto y Canada , April 1961

To A Group of 
Counsellors - In - Training 

By a Camp Director 


You are a chosen group of old 
campers, who have experienced for 
several summers all the carefree hap¬ 
piness of those, whose chief concern at 
camp, is to have a good time. Your 
days as campers are now over, and you 
are returning in a different role. You 
are to be leaders—not, perhaps, with 
all the responsibility of full-fledged 
counsellors, but certainly as counsellors- 
in-training, or “counsellors-to-be”. 

Because you have been campers and 
have a wealth of happy memories and 
many camp skills, and because you 
appreciate the high traditions and the 
aspects of good camping, I feel sure 
of your loyalty and your eagerness to 
share what you have gained with a 
younger group. Because camping is so 
essentially a real part of you, the oppor¬ 
tunity to pass on to others some of 
the joys that have been yours, will give 
you great satisfaction and scope for 
all the gifts you possess. 

The word “counsellor” is a pleasant, 
happy word. At the first camp I 
attended, the leaders were called 
“officers”. That word suggests disci¬ 
pline (and no nonsense!), with a mili¬ 
tary flavor, and a rather impersonal 
relationship. But the modern word, 
“counsellor”, suggests the friendly rela¬ 
tionship of comrade as well as leader. 

Perhaps, as you think back over 
your camp days, you can remember 
certain counsellors whom you liked 
and respected greatly. You probably 
admired them, not only for their skill 


and ability to do a good job in their 
particular field, whether it was crafts 
or swimming, music or sailing, but you 
admired them even more just for them¬ 
selves — for their friendliness, their 
dependability, their genuine interest in 
you. There were times, of course, when 
you tried to put something over on 
them, but you respected them all the 
more if they weren’t “easy”, if they 
didn’t play for popularity or shirk a 
duty because it was difficult. You knew 
that the camp director expected high 
standards from counsellors in matters of 
discipline, punctuality and cheerful, 
willing teamwork, and you were bright 
enough to know and appreciate when 
a counsellor measured up to these high 
standards. 

Now it is your turn to enter this 
role at camp—to pass on to a new and 
younger group all that has meant most 
to you. You probably realize that at 
this very moment there are swarms 
of children thinking and dreaming 
about their first days at camp. Their 
applications are in. They have read 
and re-read the folder and studied the 
pictures. They have begun to collect 
their outfit and perhaps to pack their 
belongings. Some of them may have 
mixed feelings about going to camp. 
They have heard from school friends 
and parents about the fun they are 
going to have, but they sometimes 
wonder, too, if they will be a bit lonely 
at times, for it will all be so new and 
strange. 

turn to page 135 


108 


Canadian Camping 



THE CALCULATED 


RISK 


//. M. Devenney, M.A . 


There are those philosophers who 
would say that there is a calculated risk 
in all that we do; and that as we have 
progressed in our mechanized civiliza¬ 
tion the odds of there not being risk 
are very low. Of course in relationship 
to the status quo of any community, 
learning, per se, is a calculated risk; 
that is if we think of learning as the 
process of “leading out** from the 
known to the unknown. 

Unfortunately the negative connota¬ 
tions of the word “risk” come to the 
forefront of many discussions when it 
appears. Sometimes it is used to imply 
the absence of purpose in the succes¬ 
sion of events to which it may be re¬ 
lated, or a certain precariousness is 
implied to those who take risks. 

Yet there is a most positive meaning. 
It is the meaning used in business in 
many instances, “lending on security”, 
“investing of capital” in a new project, 
“an advance on collateral”. And so we 
get the “calculated risk”, something not 
done blindly but with purpose and yet 
having within its accomplishment — 
adventure — something of a bold 
undertaking. 

The calculated risk can be the adven¬ 
ture part of camping. In order to 
understand this a little better let us dig 


a little deeper into meanings. Perhaps 
the very structure of the camping com¬ 
munity lends itself to the perpetuation 
of the calculated risk. In all too many 
situations at camp we tend to erect 
picket fences, literally or figuratively, 
around those areas of camp experience 
which have elements, the surmounting 
of which are likely to involve calcu¬ 
lated risk. These calculated risks may 
be inherent in property; they may be 
implied in programs, or they may just 
be the result of human relationships. 

Before we look more closely at the 
calculated risks in camping, let it be 
clearly understood that when we think 
of the organized camp, it should be as 
a place where sound, positive learning, 
growth and development may take 
place, provided, of course, that the en¬ 
vironment, the leadership and the ex¬ 
perience therein is all designed with 
this in mind. Remember too, that when 
and if, as has been suggested already, 
learning involves proceeding from the 
known to the unknown, especially at 
any depth, then there will be conflict. 
Learning involves “calculated risk”. 

Although adventure is not the same 
as calculated risk, it does involve cal¬ 
culated risk; and although it may not 
be called a basic need, it can be co¬ 
related with other needs. Thus in 
camping certain problems develop in 
the expression and control of adventure 
in which, if positive solutions resulting 
in learning are to develop, then a great 
measure of calculated risk is involved. 

Sometimes when this need for adven¬ 
ture is not satisfied, a highly explosive 
tension will build up. A well known 
camp authority has pin pointed ex¬ 
amples of this for us. 


Toronto , Canada , April 1961 


109 


What happnes when the wind and 
the rain have besieged you in camp for 
longer than one day? Besides damp 
shoes, feet, blankets etc., etc., damp 
spirits begin to erupt in “Fights’*. The 
“barracking” of the counsellor! Mono¬ 
tony has been dispelled. The kids have 
taken calculated risks. What about that 
last night in camp? What about the 
tensions which have been building up? 
The campers! The counsellors! The 
senior staff! The Directors! 

Unless there has been a calculated 
risk taken to forestall such high explo¬ 
sive tensions, the values which were 
confidently predicated on opening day 
would result from the stay at camp, 
will not be in evidence. Can we afford 
not to take calculated risks by not 
introducing adventure to our programs? 

Peculiarly as respects adventure, 
when the need is strong the particu¬ 
larity which we attach to its satisfaction 
is in inverse proportion, so it seems, 
to its strength. Let me illustrate by 
some of the things we sometimes hear 
at camp; and again I rely on the hu¬ 
mour of a well-known camp authority. 

“Come on now, Joe, get down off 
that cabin. You know you should not 
be up there.” Or, “You’ve had it, Bill. 
Just get right out of the water; no 
more for you today.” We all can think 
of many other kinds of ways in which 
frustrations to the secret of adventure 
—the calculated risk—have at times 
been set up in camps. A whole picket 
fence of negatives can be mentioned 
and still be but a very short list. 

Now it can be agreed upon that the 
negatives have been established for a 
purpose and the purpose is usually 
safety. To offset this kind of situation 
some camps have tried to satisfy the 
adventurous soul by providing what 
ought to be called artificial oppor¬ 
tunities. And so we see a plethora of 
Indian Tepees and Tomahawks, blunt¬ 


ed but nevertheless weapons, wampum 
belts and so on ad infinitum. This is 
play acting. This is not learning of a 
real kind. Let us not think that the 
calculated risk in which adventure is 
inherent must only depend upon tang¬ 
ibles, upon things. “Things don’t hap¬ 
pen to people, it is people who happen 
to things.” 

Calculated risk! Adventure! Fun! 
Growth and Development! Learning! 
Most certainly camping remains extant 
because in and around all that can be 
said of it, these elements are possible 
of realization. 

The hazards of the outdoors can be 
real or fancied. We in this article are 
concerned mainly with the real outdoor 
hazards because it is here that there 
can be real calculated risks. Any ex¬ 
perienced and sympathetic counsellor 
knows that the first night in camp for 
many children can be a terrifying ex¬ 
perience. In order to meet the calcu¬ 
lated risk parents and camp staff surely 
should prepare beforehand by initiating 
the neophyte through pictures, slides or 
movies of the insects or birds or mam¬ 
mals who make the night watches their 
mode of life. There are record albums 
of these voices in the night now on the 
market. The preparation for calculated 
risks can turn youngsters’ fears into 
delighted interest and mysterious foot¬ 
falls can be those of friends. 

In summation, then, it is submitted 
that whether we admit it or no, there 
will always be the calculated risk in 
camping. It should be our purpose to 
positively use it. Ignorance or just 
sheer stupidity or thoughtlessness gets 
man into most of his troubles. Inevit¬ 
ably because of all of these factors a 
high correlation exists between danger 
and adventure. But it is only as we 
utilize danger and the unexpected, ac¬ 
companied by preparation and knowl¬ 
edge that we really exploit the adven¬ 
ture potentials of our campsites and our 
leadership. —•

COOKING WITH FOIL . . . Reprinted from The Scout Leader 


Perfect meals for hike or overnight 
—no pots or pans to carry—no dishes 
to wash afterwards. How does that 
sound to you? Sweet but impossible? 
Not at all—if you go in for aluminum 
foil cookery. If you want a meal of 
meat and potatoes for instance, you 
simply wrap them in a double thick¬ 
ness of foil and place the package in 
hot coals. When done, the foil itself 
is your plate. If it’s bacon and eggs 
you desire, you crimp up the edges of 
a double sheet of foil and use that for 
a pan. If you want a cup of steaming 
cocoa you can make a pot from two 
thicknesses of foil, by folding it the 
way you fold a square of paper into 
a drinking cup, then flatten the bot¬ 
tom. The pot goes into the coals. 

Steaks, chops, fish, vegetables of all 
kinds, biscuits, short-cake, small pies, 
baked fruit—the sky’s the limit. 

The fire is the important thing! You 
need COALS — just right for the 
dish you intend to cook. At first, open 
up your package from time to time 


to check progress of the cooking and 
until eventually after a couple of times 
you become an expert. 

BAKED APPLE AND 
BAKED BANANA 

Fruit makes excellent dessert. Cut 
a “lid” off the top of an apple, re¬ 
move core, sprinkle in a teaspoon of 
sugar. Place in the middle of a piece 
of foil, bring corners up over apple, 
then twist them together. Wrap up 
banana, skin and all, in a piece of 
foil. Place wrapped up fruit in hot 
coals. Apple bakes in about 30 minutes, 
banana in 10 minutes. Serve in the 
foil. 

Aluminum foil may be bought in 
most hardware, grocery and depart¬ 
ment stores. It comes in boxes like 
waxed paper 12 inches wide, 75 feet 
long. Instead of taking a whole roll 
hiking, cut off what you need. Fold 
up “utensils” in advance and throw 
them in your rucsac. Most dishes can 
be fixed at home. 

—• 


Toronto . Canada, April 1961

HOW WE . . . 

COPE WITH STAFF RECREATION 

Ron Johnstone , London YMCA 


London YMCA-YWCA operates Camp Queen Elizabeth on Beausoleil Island 
in Georgian Bay, near Honey Harbour. The Camp has a staff of fourteen coun¬ 
sellors, nine program specialists and nine service and medical staff. Since the 
staff is a relatively small and cohesive group, the majority of the in-camp recrea¬ 
tion is informal and centers around the staff lounge with its books and its record 
player. 

A Junior Honey Harbour Association was formed on a co-operative basis 
with the young people of the District. The association has two main functions, 
firstly, to operate a good quality young people’s dance and recreation program 
three times per week and secondly, to sponsor the local August 1st Regatta. The 
Camp co-operates on both of these projects. 

This organization gives our staff an excellent opportunity for fellowship on 
their days off. Those off duty on the dance nights have the privilege of attending 
a good quality dance with their own age group. 

The first Association party is held each year in the Camp Rec. Hall in the 
week before Camp starts. This party usually has 80 - 90 district young people in 
attendance. It takes the form of a dance party followed by cocoa and cookies 
with a song-fest around the fire to close off. We have found that the district young 
people have developed a great interest and respect for the Camp. The party 
enables our staff to renew old acquaintances and make new friends. 

On the alternate dance nights one of the local lodges operates program 
and welcomes our staff participation. I might stress that considerable effort has 
gone into insuring and promoting the good name and reputation of the Camp and 
the Camp Staff. 

In-Camp recreation is directed by the Senior Staff and twice weekly special 
‘feeds’ and programs are planned. These usually take the form of party games 
and often close around the fireplace with quiet songs and discussion. 

The camping day is organized and busy. The busiest people in camp are 
the counsellors. By mutual agreement our counsellors have decided that they 
should be early to bed before any day off since the next night is liable to be a late 
one. We are constantly battling fatigue even in our senior staff. We recognize, 
to do a complete camping job, that full rest is vitally important. With this in 
mind our usual evenings are very relaxing and the staff is in bed by 11:30 p.m. and 
usually before. This bed time is a staff council decision. 

A minimum of planned recreation is needed. I believe that in a Camp, of 
this size, that the responsibility for staff recreation lies with the director and the 
staff council. Since a well-rested happy staff is necessary for a well-operated 
Camping program this business of staff recreation should be of major impor¬ 
tance to the Camp Director, and not just another incidental item of operation.

Canadian Camping 



HOW WE . . . 

COPE WITH DETAILS 

Elizabeth W. Raymer 
Camp Tanamakoon 


In addition to the overall detailed organization of a camp for a smooth 
running season, there is a welter of unclassifiable, almost microscopic detail which 
must be covered by the directors. Sometimes a seemingly small thing, if over¬ 
looked, can create confusion and inconvenience. The method described here can 
be adapted to cover any department of camp supervision. In this example we 
are concerned with details which a camp director wishes to make known to coun¬ 
sellors and campers. 

Before camp opens in 1961 take a loose-leaf notebook and prepare one page 
for each day of the season, including pre-camp and post-camp. Jot down under 
the appropriate date every conceivable item which will require attention. After 
camp is in session keep the notebook handy and enter anything which comes to 
your notice. 

Every day, consult your notebook and no matter how busy you are, you will 
be able to prepare a calm and collected agenda. You will of course have your 
own mechanics for communicating this information to counsellors and campers, 
(Someone should write an article!) 

At the conclusion of the camp season do not cast this notebook aside. Pre¬ 
serve it carefully and use it for reference in making up your notebook for 1962. 

Here is an example:— 


Counsellors 

1. Buffet supper tomorrow 
Procedure, serving, clean up. 

2. Tomorrow change seating in dining 
room. New lists ready today. 

3. Campers’ laundry goes out today. 

4. Parents visiting today— 

Mr. and Mrs. James 
Mrs. Henry 

5. Repairs—any broken beds in camp? 

6. Advance notice — Park Naturalists 
will be here July 14th. 

7. Are all safety rules being observed? 


Campers 

Buffet supper tomorrow—how we 
do it. 

New table lists posted before dinner. 
Your laundry goes out today. Be 
sure to observe all your counsellor’s 
instructions. 

Aerosol containers — where to put 
empty ones. 

Talk on Tonakela in preparation 
for Sunday offering. 

Did anyone hear the owl last night? 
Council fire tonight. Bring blanket, 
ground sheet and flashlight. 

Have you collected ideas for your 
Sunday letter home?

TO SPRAY 

or ROT to SPRAY ... 


Audubon Society of Canada 


Few conservation questions of our 
tune have attracted more attention than 
the modern practice of broadcasting 
highly toxic chemicals in efforts to con¬ 
trol nuisance insects and other forms of 
life. The interest of Audubon Society 
in this matter centres about the effects 
of pesticides on wildlife. 

Man has to a very great measure 
become the manipulator of his own 
environment. Sometimes, in the best 
interest of human affairs, it is necessary 
to take local control measures against 
forms that become super-abundant. 
The use of toxic chemicals as one form 
of control has become established, and 
it is here to stay. 

The concern of many conservation¬ 
ists over chemical pesticides is not in 
the poisons themselves, but rather in 
some of the methods of their applica¬ 
tion, and also in a potentially dangerous 
philosophy which has developed within 
the period of their increasingly wide¬ 
spread use. In the minds of far too 
many people, pesticides have become a 
sort of panacea for all that ails the 
field, the forest, the vegetable garden. 
This apparently growing blind faith in 
chemical poisons has often led to their 
use without adequate prior considera¬ 
tion of the risks involved. 

Research in this field is very limited, 
particularly in Canada. From what has 
been learned already, however, it is safe 
to say that the indiscriminate and 


wholesale use of chemical pesticides 
could represent one of the most sweep¬ 
ing threats to wildlife yet experienced 
in human history. Shockingly great 
kills of invertebrates, fishes, birds and 
other animals as the result of careless 
or massive spraying programs are well 
documented.* 

Some destruction of wildlife has been 
the result of direct toxicity—the poison¬ 
ing of animals other than or in addition 
to the target species. Some has resulted 
from the elimination of food supply. 
Even more dangerous, however, may be 
the long-term cumulative effects of 
some chemicals, including chlorinated 
hydrocarbons of the DDT group. Re¬ 
peated sub-lethal doses of some of these 
preparations can accumulate in living 
tissue, with effects that can be seen 
later in reproductive success, viability 
of offspring, etc. Still other effects can 
be seen in natural “food-chains”. 

One example of this has been care¬ 
fully worked out in connection with 
DDT spraying for Dutch elm disease. 
Poison is left on the leaves of the trees; 
the leaves fall to the ground in the 
autumn; earthworms eat the leaf litter, 
absorbing the poison; the following 
spring the still-living earthworms are 
eaten by robins; the robins die of DDT 
poisoning. In Michigan and elsewhere, 
whole local populations of robins have 
been wiped out in this way. Fish¬ 
eating birds have also been eliminated 
in regions where heavy spraying pro- 


118 


Canadian Camping 



grams have been conducted. They ac¬ 
quired the poison through eating con¬ 
taminated fish. 

There is a mounting body of evidence 
of reproductive failure in birds due to 
exposure of insecticides. Accumula¬ 
tions of poison have been found in the 
reproductive organs of both captive and 
wild birds. Laboratory tests with phea¬ 
sants and quail have shown that expo¬ 
sure to chemical pesticides can result in 
a drop in egg production, a drop in 
egg fertility, and an increase in chick 
mortality. 

Unfortunately, most research and 
other investigation into the problem 
has been after the fact, rather than 
before it. Damage to wildlife has usu¬ 
ally been assessed following a spray 
program, and there has been insuffi¬ 
cient attempt made to gauge the hazard 
in advance, through controlled experi¬ 
mentation. 

In the final analysis, the only lasting 
and harmless checks on “pest” species 


will be those in which we put nature 
to work, in the form of parasites, pre¬ 
dators, and other biological agents. 
Some extremely interesting research is 
going forward in this direction, and 
some fascinating techniques are now 
being worked out. However, until we 
have adequate biological controls avail¬ 
able, we must keep a close watch over 
the careless or indiscriminate use of 
pesticides. 

If we do not exercise extreme care, 
we could bring about a catastrophic 
state of natural imbalance. Its effects 
could well be much more serious than 
the depredations of the animals we now 
seek (so often in futility) to control 
through chemical poisons. If we must 
use toxic chemicals, let us remember 
that pinpointed rifle shooting is much 
more selective than massive, all-inclu¬ 
sive shotgun fire. 

*—See “Canadian Audubon” maga¬ 
zine, Mar .-Apr., 1961. Audubon Society 
of Canada, 423 Sherbourne Street, 
Toronto 5. 




HE FOLLOWED INSTRUCTIONS 

The Washington Biological Society, which puis metal bands on wild birds to study 
their migratory habits, recently ordered new bands with different and more detailed wording. 

The new metal bands now read, “Notify Fish and Wildlife Services, Washington, D.C” 
Formerly , the bands said simply, “Wash. Biol. Suru” 

UnofficiaTexplanation of the change is that an irate citizen 9 s letter complained: “Sir, 
I shot down one of your pet crows, and followed instructions. I washed it, biled it, and 
surved it. It was terrible. Stop fooling the people!” 

—Reprinted from Sylva Magazine .

"FOOTPRINTS 


on 


the Sands of Time 


// 


Reprinted from 
The Young Naturalist 


A collection of plaster casts of 
tracks can be made with very little 
skill or equipment, and it provides a 
splendid object for outdoors activities. 

Even around towns and cities there 
are many creatures which leave the 
impression of their feet in their wan¬ 
derings. The best place to find these 
tracks is in the smooth mud on the 
banks of streams, or the level surface 
of the wave-washed sand beaches. Of 
course, freshly-fallen snow reveals the 
most, but as you will see, such tracks 
do not suit our purpose for the time 
being at least. 

A good way to secure tracks and 
trails is to smooth out a level area 
either on mud or sand and bait it with 
a scrap of meat. Then visit the spot 
the following morning for the story of 
what happened during the night. 

When you have selected the impres¬ 
sion you want from several tracks 
which may be left, carefully pick out 
any twigs or leaves, then surround it 
with wall or fence of strips of card¬ 
board, either in circle or rectangle, at 
a reasonable distance from the track. 
Into one side of this pour a mixture 
of plaster of paris in form of batter, 
and let flow over the track. This bat¬ 
ter should be thin enough to pour 
freely and thick enough to settle 
evenly and quickly. You can make it 
settle well into all the lines and creases 
of the track by patting the plaster 


lightly as if you were making a mud 
pie. The semi-fluid batter ought to 
settle and harden in about 10 minutes, 
especially on a sunny day. 

When set, carefully lift the cast out 
of the wall and allow it to dry com¬ 
pletely. A little gentle heating at 
home later will hasten this. Of course 
some of the mud or sand will be found 
clinging to the cast and this can be 
taken off carefully with running water. 
Now trim off the whole piece and you 
will have a replica of the track made 
by the animal. 

But your trophy is still only half- 
made, for this replica is all in reverse 
—it is raised where the animal made 
hollows. You must reverse your own 
work to get back to the original. When 
the cast is thoroughly dry smear grease 
or vaseline over the surface and wipe 
it off well, leaving a thin film of grease, 
so thin that none of the delicate 
wrinkles or lines of the track are filled 
up. This greasing is very important. 
Without it the two casts stick firmly 
together and cannot be separated. Now 
around the trimmed edges fasten a wall 
as you did in the mud or sand and 
pour over it a second batter of plaster 
of paris. Tap the whole lightly so it 
will settle down and let dry until 
quite hard. Now with a thin knife 
carefully separate the two casts and 
you will have a perfect impression of 
the animal’s track you found outdoors. 

—•

NEWS . . 


from the Provinces 


JOINT CHARTER — QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION INC.— 

L’ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU QUEBEC INC. 

The Quebec Camping Association formed on February 11, 1937, had been 
planning for some time to apply for incorporation and become a chartered affiliate 
of the Canadian Camping Association (originally founded in Toronto in 1936), 
when it learned that the French group—L* Association des Camps du Quebec— 
founded about three years ago, were interested in joining with them in obtaining 
a Charter. Both groups recognized that a united and incorporated group could 
be of mutual benefit and accomplish more for the camping movement in any 
contacts with Provincial Government Departments. 

Early in June, 1960, the first steps were taken towards incorporation of the 
Association to be known as “Quebec Camping Association Inc.—L’Association 
des Camps du Quebec Inc.”, and during the summer all legal points were studied 
and settled. There was great rejoicing in Quebec when the Application for the 
Charter was finally completed and signed on November 26, 1960, at a Conference 
held by the French Section. The Application for the Charter was signed by Mrs. 
Alta R. Kahn, President, Quebec Camping Association, Mr. Kenneth Murray, 
immediate Past-President, L’Abbe Raoul Cloutier. Priest and Director of Camp- 
Ecole Trois-Saumons, and Mr. Rene Saint-Onge, President, L*Association des 
Camps du Quebec. On November 28, 1960, formal application was made and on 
January 9, 1961, we received notification that the granting of the Charter had 
been approved. Thus another chapter in the history of camping in the Province 
of Quebec has been written. The English and French Sections will each operate 
independently but will have a joint Board to deal with matters affecting the 
whole camping movement in the Province of Quebec. 

This achievement augurs well for the future of camping in the Province of 
Quebec and is the culmination of two years of effort on the part of the Charter 
Committee under the Chairmanship of Mr. Ernie Freedman, ably assisted by Mr. 
Tony Shorgan, Mr. Kenneth Murray, L’Abbe Raoul Cloutier, Mrs. Alta R. Kahn 
and Mr. F. M. Van Wagner, President, Canadian Camping Association, whose 
advice and counsel helped immeasurably in this effort. 


Toronto , Canada , April 1961

INDIAN 

DAY 

Ontario Camp 

for Retarded Children 

by June Braaten, Camp Director 


It is 2:00 p.m. Almost everything is 
in readiness for the long awaited Indian 
Day at Camp Belwood, where sixty 
seriously retarded boys from all parts 
of Ontario have come to spend three 
happy weeks. It is rest hour, and all 
is quiet. 

The Ontario Association for Retard¬ 
ed Children administers this Camp on 
a site loaned by the Guelph Kiwanis 
Club. It is also subsidized by a gener¬ 
ous grant from the Ontario Lodges and 
Chapters, Loyal Order of Moose. The 
youngest campers who are eight years 
old are asleep, and even the oldest 
campers of eighteen years are resting, 
for these youngsters are not used to the 
amount of fine physical activity that 
this camp provides regularly each day 
in the program — tumbling, learning 
games’ skills, hiking and swimming. 
There is more than one reason why they 
do not have as much exercise as other 
children. 

At home, because their handicap 
makes it impossible for them to “keep 
up”, most have never played success¬ 
fully with neighbourhood children of 


their own age. The need for constant 
supervision also prevents them from 
being allowed to romp with the gang. 
Instead they sit looking at TV or, from 
a window or porch, watching other 
children play. Another possibility for 
exercise, just walking to school, is not 
even for them. The fact that this one 
per cent of our population is scattered 
throughout the community necessitates 
that they be picked up and brought 
home in taxis or buses from their spe¬ 
cial schools. Thus, these children need 
very badly the kind of active program 
a good camp can provide. However, 
at first they become tired easily, so 
rest must be provided. They must 
have their rest hour, even on this ex¬ 
citing day. It is essential. 

The counsellors and senior staff are 
not resting on this day, however. This 
climactic Indian pow-wow has special 
meaning for them. Every ounce of 
energy is going into making this the 
best day ever for the campers whom 
they have grown to love! These dedi¬ 
cated young people, with a spirit for 
adventure, and the desire to do some¬ 
thing for a handicapped child, have 
come to Camp Belwood. Most of them 
have had no previous experience with 
retarded children, but have been camp 
counsellors before. The Ontario Asso¬ 
ciation for Retarded Children is grate¬ 
ful to these young people who have had 
experience at other Ontario camps, for 
it is obvious that this Association does 
not have the happy situation of “being 
able to grow its own staff” from its 
campers. The fine training course at 
the Ontario Dept, of Education camp 
at Bark Lake is a great help too. 

One of the counsellors in each cabin 
(which houses two counsellors and six 
campers) is quietly checking the cos¬ 
tumes which each of his three campers 
has prepared with much help, during 
craft periods. Counsellors must super¬ 
vise their own campers at all times with 


124 


Canadian Camping 


the exception of rest hour, when one 
counsellor may stay with the six camp¬ 
ers, or in the evening when there is a 
patrol. So, at this time, the other coun¬ 
sellor in each cabin is out performing 
one of the many last minute duties, 
such as finishing the tribal sign painted 
on heavy craft paper, for the outside of 
the cabin; assisting the Nature Lore 
Director to check the fireplaces which 
each program group prepared for 
the Indian feast during the previous 
day’s hike on the lakeshore; helping 
the Craft Director mix the lard and 
gaudily coloured tempera make-up for 
the older braves, and just plain tem¬ 
pera for the younger braves; checking 
the routine for the Indian fire dance 
with the Dramatics Director (a very 
simple version had been practiced and 
practiced in the dramatics period— 
repetition being an important principle 
in a retarded child’s learning) ; putting 
the final touches to small plaster of 
paris circular moulds, on which is 
painted the various tribal signs, and 
which are destined to be presented to 
all the braves later; collecting the props 
for the Games Director’s session of 
Indian Games, or checking the lean-to 
of heavy craft paper which has been 
painted with Indian signs, laced be¬ 
tween a frame of branches and made 
to stand behind each of the tribal fire¬ 
places, which have been prepared 
around the main ceremonial fire. 

The Director and Program Director 
have checked the whole schedule and 
are busy getting into their own cos¬ 
tumes which were made at a staff- 
bee late last night. 

The moment has arrived. The wake- 
up whistle sounds, and suddenly peace 
is supplanted by the sound of excited 
voices asking questions. Knowing 
counsellors insist that campers must 
wash as usual. Then costumes are 
donned with much glee. Senior staff 
arrive at the cabins with the make-up 


on trays. Someone carries a mirror 
(the retarded child must see to under¬ 
stand. His physical senses are the 
means by which he learns). What fun 
to get painted! And when his counsel¬ 
lor dons the war paint, too, his joy is 
complete. Finally, everyone is ready. 
The Great Chief (Program Director) 
and other senior staff, and kitchen 
staff in costume proceed solemnly in 
single file to the central area. They 
begin a circle around the flag-pole. 
The Chief utters a thunderous call. The 
braves answer and proceed to the circle. 
When all have assembled, the entire 
nation begins a slow dance around the 
pole. They stop at a sign from the 
Great Chief, who turns, faces the great 
totem and exclaims, “O Great Mani- 
tou, bless us in our Indian games”. 
After kneeling and bowing once, the 
Chief exclaims, “Go, braves. Let the 
Belwood games begin.” 

For a gay hour, the braves proceed in 
single file, Indian style from one game 
to the next, until each group has par¬ 
ticipated in five Indian games. (Even 
this simple routine has taken two weeks 
to master in dramatics periods). The 
staff remembers that, on this exciting 
day, they must include some of the 
regular camp routines, for routine is 
the foundation on which the retarded 
child’s learning is built, and from 
whence a feeling of security comes. 
Now the time has come when even an 
Indian brave must go to the wash¬ 
room. 

Soon all the tribes are gathered at 
the dining hall door. They chant an 
Indianized version of “Cumbiah Lord”. 
It was learned in sing-song period, first 
very slowly and bit by bit, but in the 
end even seriously retarded children 
know the words and sing, not all in 
tune, but in time. 

The kitchen staff, who have all fallen 
in love with their family of campers. 


Toronto , Canada , April 1961 


125 




pass out the boxes of food. The tribes 
then file down to the shore where the 
special fireplaces are ready for cooking 
the feast of: 

Roast Potatoes (baked in oven, but now 
thrown into ashes for effect) 

Corn-on-the Cob (pre-cooked but still 
in 105 oz. cans with some boiling 
water—to be placed on the stones 
near the fire) 

Venison (hunks of Kam to be roasted 
on sticks, which have been procured 
previously on a nature-hike) 

Fire Water (fruit drink in bottle jugs) 
Bananas (real bananas) 

Cookies and buttered bread (filler- 
uppers) 

After another familiar wash-room 
routine, the braves are ready once again 
for the evening council ring. One of 
each of the cabin counsellors has taken 
blankets enough for his cabin tribe and 
placed them by their lean-to. Even on 
this special day, he remembers that it 
is important to see that his campers do 
not take a chill in the cool night air, 
for they (especially the mongoloids) 
are very susceptible to respiratory in¬ 
fection. 

The tribes gather, each in a single 
line, on the hilltop overlooking the 
scene for the ceremonial fire. It is dusk 
and the sky on this night of nights is 
filled with all the colours of a glorious 
sunset, as if reflecting the many hues 
of the braves’ war paint. 

The ceremony for the gathering of 
the tribes is about to begin. Princess 
Happy Fire (one of the kitchen girls) 
lights a roman candle by each tribal fire 
in turn, as Chief Big Noise (Craft 
Director) beats on a huge decorated 
drum. The Great Chief calls “How”. 
Each tribe in turn calls back “How” 
and proceeds to his place around his 
own fire. The braves are not afraid 
but full of awe in the presence of this 
ritual, just as any other children would 
be. They are silent. 


The torchbearers (senior staff and 
two counsellors) enter. They are bene¬ 
volent medicine men. Around the tribes 
they circle, their bodies bending and 
swaying with their torches. They touch 
each tribal fireplace with their torches. 
Now all the tribal fires are blazing. 
They pass again dropping powder on 
each fire. Now the flames arc blue in 
the gathering darkness. 

The torchbearers, torches held high, 
turn their eyes to the lake. What do 
they see? — a boat approaches. They 
run to the water’s edge and light the 
way for the boat—a boat which moves 
without oarsmen (counsellors are swim¬ 
ming and pushing the boat), in the 
helm of which stands a white goddess. 
They assist her to shore, (the Camp 
Director has changed to the white gown 
of an Indian goddess) and escort her 
to the great totem. The goddess speaks 
to the Indian nation and expresses, in 
very simple language, her pleasure at 
the fine behaviour of all the braves and 
blesses them all. The braves in turn 
sing “We are the Redmen” then “Jesus 
Loves the Little Children of the World” 
(a favourite in their Sunday service). 

Now the moment has arrived when 
each tribe gives thanks to the gods. 
Each group has painstakingly practiced 
a very simple dance for almost three 
weeks, just one step but it is enough 
and very effective, because this simple 
dance, which seemed nothing much in 
Dramatics periods, now is combined 
with the night, the fire, the war paint, 
costumes and a background of Indian 
chiefs, medicine men and Indian 
maidens. The “Spear Tribe” is first 
to present its dance. At the end, they 
throw their spears beyond the totem. 
Each tribe in turn performs its simple 
dance and offers its gift at the totem. 
In between dances there are special 
features. The Director portrays an 
Indian Maiden, “Little White Dove” 

turn to page 138

Canadian Camping 




from page 101 

posing the camper to the best possible 
environment in which these apprecia¬ 
tions can be fostered. 

The physical setting of the camp can 
do much toward this end. Spreading 
out camp buildings and retaining much 
of the natural setting about them is 
but one example of how this might be 
accomplished. Locating campfire areas 
with an excellent view of the lake at 
sundown is another. 

Subtle planning on the part of those 
in charge of program may be the key 
to strengthening the youngster’s aware¬ 
ness of the beauty of nature. Experi¬ 
enced campfire leaders know, for ex¬ 
ample, that small campfire groups are 
better than large ones, and that the 
more boisterous part of the campfire 
program should be planned for the 
early part of the evening. 

In attempting to evaluate what the 
camper expects of camp, our list could 
be extended indefinitely. The author 
has chosen to mention but four which 
he believes stand high on the camper’s 
list. Unless we can truthfully say that 
camp fulfills each of these wants in 
some good measure, there must be 
serious questions as to whether we have 
the right to use the phrase “camp 
experience”.

WHAT IS 
DAY 

CAMPING? 

Eleanor Reesor, 

Chairman of Social Planning Council 
Day Camp Committee 


Day Camping is an organized camp¬ 
ing program carried on under qualified 
leadership in a permanent, outdoor 
campsite e.g., a park, wooded ravine, 
shady hill area on a farm, or in a quiet 
wood. 

As its name implies, the Day Camp¬ 
ers travel to and from the designated 
campsite each week day for an estab¬ 
lished period of one, two or more 
weeks. Special “sleep-outs”, usually 
one per camp period, provide the only 
occasion for staying overnight on the 
campsite or in some other suitable loca¬ 
tion. Some Day Camp Directors prefer 
to leave this “sleeping out” experience 
to Residence Camps. 

During the past twenty-five years, 
there has been a phenomenal growth 
in the Day Camp movement in all parts 
of Canada and the United States. 

Day Camps are usually sponsored by 
“non-profit” organizations such as set¬ 
tlement houses, churches, Y.M.C.A.’s, 
Y.W.C.A.’s, Y.M.-Y.W.H.A.’s, service 
clubs and municipal recreation depart¬ 
ments. Sometimes two of these groups 


will combine to be co-sponsors of cer¬ 
tain Day Camps, e.g. a service club may 
totally finance one camp period, or 
more commonly choose to underwrite 
specific costs such as rentals of swim¬ 
ming pools, or to provide arts and craft 
supplies or free milk. 

There are three major reasons 
for organizations requiring financial 
support from interested community 
groups: 

(1) Operating costs for Day Camps, 
like everything else, have risen steadily 
in recent years, especially the bus trans¬ 
portation to and from the most desir¬ 
able out-of-town campsites. Ironically, 
as a big city grows, Day Camp operators 
have to travel farther and farther away 
in order to find suitable sites for good 
Day Camp programs. 

(2) Voluntary agencies like the 
three Y’s and settlement houses or the 
municipal recreation departments don’t 
want to make money on their Day 
Camps, but they do have to break even; 
therefore, to keep the camp fees low 
enough for the children who need camp 
most , many Day Camps have operating 
deficits. Here is where additional finan¬ 
cial support is urgently needed from 
service clubs or any interested indi¬ 
viduals. 

(3) Any voluntary agency or muni¬ 
cipal recreation department welcomes 
interest and support from groups or 
individuals in their “home” communi¬ 
ties. Naturally, the more people who 
really know about our important Day 
Camp programs, the better is the com¬ 
munity’s understanding of the value of 
day camping generally. 

It is unfortunate that some organiza¬ 
tions unwittingly confuse their “vaca¬ 
tion, summer fun, or stay-at-home” 
clubs with bona-fide Day Camps. A 
playground program or regular winter 
program activities merely transplanted 
out-of-doors into the playground, back- 


128 




Canadian Camping 



yard or even centred in the building it¬ 
self are not true Day Camping pro¬ 
grams. 

Day Camp is a well-organized camp¬ 
ing program separate unto itself, with 
trained leadership and small groups of 
children of the same age, guided by the 
same adult counsellor for each camp 
period. 

What are some of the values of a 
good Day Camp program? Tradition¬ 
ally, Day Camping is an out-door pro¬ 
gram for small groups of children. It 
provides an opportunity for boys and 
girls to develop some camping skills 
and serves as an introduction to resi¬ 
dence camping, at a minimal cost. (Day 
Camp fees range from $2.50 - $9.00 
per week, which covers transportation, 
swimming, craft supplies and fresh milk 
every noon hour.) 

Within the last three or four years, 
“private” Day Camps have made their 
appearance on the local scene of some 
big Canadian cities. These camps are 
operated, as any business, for a profit, 
and their fees sometimes run as high as 
$30 per week. In fairness, it must be 
reported that some of these “private” 
Day Camps offer more elaborate facili¬ 
ties and older, better-paid counsellors. 

Day Camping, in my opinion, can 
serve as a wonderful introduction to 
the fuller experience of going away to 
stay at a Residence Camp. As a result 
of good Day Camp experience, I be¬ 
lieve that more and more Canadian 
boys and girls will be oriented to the 
joys of outdoor living and will want to 
try Residence Camps when older (the 
children, not the camps). 

The Directors and Staff of both 
Day and Residence Camps share many 
hopes and goals in common for their 
campers. They both try to run “camp¬ 
er-centred” programs, guarding against 
intensely competitive approaches to 


teaching specific skills. Conversely, they 
both realize that children need plenty 
of opportunities under skilled and sym¬ 
pathetic instruction to learn new skills. 
Children usually welcome the adven¬ 
ture, achievement, recognition, self- 
confidence and fun which skills can 
bring to them. Hopefully, the directors 
and camp staffs, in either setting, recog¬ 
nize that children have many different 
kinds of needs, e.g., intellectual, emo¬ 
tional and social, as well as the more 
evident physical needs; both staffs have 
as their objectives, the health, happiness 
and physical safety at all times of the 
campers under their supervision and 
care. 

Many Day Camp directors acknowl¬ 
edge their indebtedness to the more 
experienced Residence Camp person¬ 
nel, who have so generously shared 
their knowledge and rich experience in 
Camp Planning Programs , good health 
and safety standards and the import¬ 
ance of training both before camp and 
later, on the job, for counsellors. Just 
how Day Camps have adapted some of 
these basic principles to their own 
unique setting will be covered by suc¬ 
ceeding writers in this new series of 
articles on Day Camping. 

The average age range for day camp¬ 
ers is eight to twelve years. However, 
some Day Camp directors, either from 
conviction or budget problems, may 
stretch the minimum to six and the 
maximum to fourteen. If the campers 
are under six , I really feel that it is 
little more than an outdoor baby-sitting 
service. The psychologists agree that 
under six, most boys and girls are not 
ready for an organized group experi¬ 
ence lasting for any substantial period 
of time. Certainly some six year olds 
mav play some group games together 
quite happily, for an hour or two at a 
birthday party, but a special social oc¬ 
casion like a party, is a far cry from a 
full day of seven hours of varied pro- 


T or onto, Canada , April 1961 


129 



gram at Day Camp. However, we are 
all familiar with the extenuating cir¬ 
cumstances which accompany any pol¬ 
icy or rule, and when a prospective 
Day Camper’s parents have family 
problems of ill health, recent opera¬ 
tions, a death in the family or more 
cheerfully, a new baby at home, camp 
directors should and do, I’m sure, give 
special consideration to such individual 
cases. 

Some parents and educators favour 
“separate sex” Day Camps for boys and 
girls, believing that during the ages 
from eight to twelve, one of the devel¬ 
opment tasks in Professor Havinghurst’s 
list, is “for a child to develop an ap¬ 
propriate feminine or masculine role,” 
naturally, while the child struggles to 
sort out for himself or herself “what it 
really means to be a boy or girl”. This 
process is facilitated by close, living 
experience with other children and 
adults of the same sex. This is why 
most qualified camp directors prefer to 


have male counsellors with boys and 
female counsellors with girls—healthy, 
happy, well-adjusted men and women 
who enjoy being male or female, and 
who do not secretly or overtly wish 
that they had been born into the oppo¬ 
site sex. Growing boys and girls need 
good adult leaders of their own sex to 
identify with. 

Some camps for boys err seriously in 
this, I believe, when they hire teen- 
aged girls to act as counsellors with 
eight to twelve year old boys, merely 
because these girls will work for less 
money than male counsellors. 

Previously, I said that both Day and 
Residence Camp Directors hold many 
goals and objectives in common . 

In closing may I point out 
some of the unique values of Day 
Camping:—It provides an excellent 
introduction to outdoor living for young 
city children, some of whom will never

get away to any Residence Gamp. It 
provides a very helpful introduction to 
camping in general and teaches some 
of the beginning camping skills, e.g., 
learning to swim, tracking, outdoor 
cooking, etc. It allows many young 
girls and boys to have some camping 
experience and still be able to go away 
with their families on vacation. It al¬ 
lows older boys who have paper routes 
or week-end delivery jobs to come to 
Day Camp and still hold their jobs. 
This same value holds for older girls 
who may be needed by their mothers 
after camp to help out with light house¬ 
hold chores or to share in the care of 
younger brothers and sisters. Day 
Camping is relatively inexpensive, so it 
is possible for more boys and girls to 
attend Camp and for a longer period 
of time. 

Many city children have little oppor¬ 
tunity to learn to appreciate the beau¬ 
ties of Nature and to protect and con¬ 
serve them. Nature’s laws is one of 
the richest and most significant by¬ 
products of any good camping experi¬ 
ence. This love of Nature shows 
through one of the Y.W.C.A. Day 
Camp Reports which came to my desk 
in 1959, from Mrs. Judith Sule, Day 
Camp Director “par excellence”. “Our 
campsite is a truly natural forest, situ¬ 
ated on Manse Road, in West Hill. It 
has tall trees, a happy, little clean 
creek, hills and valleys which are a joy 
to explore and on occasion are inhabit¬ 
ed by fat rabbits, curious raccoons, dis¬ 
gusted blue jays and inquisitive squir¬ 
rels who appeared regularly to share 
Inuches with our girls”. 

From even this brief, delightful ex¬ 
cerpt, one knows immediately that here 
is a Day Camp Director who loves her 
campers, her job and all of the infinite 
wonders of the beautiful world around 
her. 

Good health and sunny weather to 
all Canadian Campers in 1961!

No doubt, the initial and immediate 
reaction to the prospect of survival 
camping may be somewhat unfavor¬ 
able. It is admitted at the outset, that 
few campers will likely be faced with a 
need to exist in the wilderness without 
regular food sources. Nonetheless, this 
possibility, although remote, is real. 
Men of the Armed Forces and anyone 
who has been lost in the woods would 
verify the need for some knowledge and 
skill in survival for emergencies. 

The real value, however, lies essen¬ 
tially in the sense of adventure aroused, 
and in the motivation created for cam¬ 
pers to familiarize themselves with the 
natural surroundings. Wildlife, wood- 
lore. campcraft, orienteering and con¬ 
servation take on new dimensions 
through survival camping. Natural 
foods obviously cannot be contemplated 
without a very thorough knowledge of 
flora and fauna, their possibilities and 
limitations. In survival camping, it 
must be acknowledged that food is a 
very basic item. Similarly it follows 
that any of the more creative methods 
of campcraft become important in such 
camping. For example, it may be nec¬ 
essary to start a fire without matches or 
to boil water in a container made from 
natural objects or to devise ways and 
means of finding and preparing food, 
shelter, or even protective clothing. 

Furthermore, the problems of survi¬ 
val become very real to participants in 
this aspect of camping. It might well 
be anticipated that a far greater interest 
in orienteering and woodlore should re¬ 
sult. The true value of a compass with 
the protection and opportunities it 
offers must certainly be realized in this 
context. In short, it can be expected 
that campers will gain a new enthusi¬ 
asm in camping activities which did not 
appear to be practical and useful for 
regular camping. 


Survival 

Campiny 


Kirk A. W. W ip per 
Camp Kandalore 



The difficulties inherent in being lost 
also demonstrate the importance of not 
getting lost. A camper does learn that 
there are risks and hazards involved in 
careless management in the wilderness. 
This too can be counted as a useful pro¬ 
duct of survival. Conservation of natur¬ 
al resources should also receive more 
attention from campers who indulge in 
this experience. Obviously indifference 
to intelligent protection of flora and 


132 


Canadian Camping 



fauna may lead to depletion of natural 
things essential to survival. 

Attitudes resulting from survival 
camping cannot be disregarded. There 
is a unique feeling of realizing one’s 
very definite dependence on the natural 
world; it is a sensation of indescribable 
effect. Here terms are reduced to fun¬ 
damentals and the individual invariably 
becomes grateful indeed, for the gener¬ 
osity of the environment. Of course, 
this inspiration is only available to those 
who can muster the utmost imagina¬ 
tion, initiative and resourcefulness. It 
is an adventure as long as the partici¬ 
pant can meet the challenge adequately. 
However, the adventure becomes hard¬ 
ship if the survival camper fails to meet 
the situation with intelligence, courage, 
skill and experience. 

Survival camping is not entirely a 
serious affair. In the pursuit of each 
day’s means for livelihood, many hilari¬ 
ous predicaments arise. The simple ob¬ 
jective of capturing and finding food 
without standard equipment leads to 
extremely funny incidents. Only those 
willing to attempt this unique kind of 
camping may enjoy the sheer fun of it 
all. A sense of humour is, indeed, an 

Finally it should be pointed out that 
unseasoned, inexperienced campers 
should not be encouraged to attempt 
survival camping. This is a privilege 
for those who have made adequate pre¬ 
paration over a reasonable period of 
time. The excerpt which follows does 
suggest something of the unique adven¬ 
ture of survival camping and does 
demonstrate that any investment of 
time and effort in this sort of camping 
is appropriately rewarded. 

VOYAGE MERGANSER 

“During the first week of September 
1960, two Norwesters “lived off the 
land” in Algonquin Park (Permission 


from the proper authorities was ob¬ 
tained). This was not a sudden im¬ 
pulse or an idea conceived in a moment 
of foolhardiness, but rather a well 
thought out survival expedition. Since 
both members shared a fetish for the 
great outdoors, they spent the summer 
teaching survival methods such as iden¬ 
tifying edible plant and animal life, 
primitive fire methods, natural shelters 
and birchbark utensils. However, they 
were anxious to put their knowledge to 
the test under proper circumstances. 
So, setting out with just an axe, a knife, 
some piano wire (for snares) and a few 
miscellaneous articles such as pen and 
paper for the log, they began a seven 
day trip. All articles such as food and 
matches were strictly tabooed. 

“Reaching their chosen destination, 
a remote arm of Timberwolf Lake, thev 
proceeded to set up a base camp. 

“A suitable location was found on a 
very heavily wooded point. They con¬ 
structed there a shelter from spruce 
poles and lashed them with watap 
(peeled spruce roots). Balsam bows 
were spread lavishly over the small flat 
floor to ensure good sleeping (which 
incidentally is very important). Their 
first meal consisted of a duck which 
was killed by a thrown stone, and boiled 
cattail roots which are a good potato 
substitute. Future meals consisted of 
such delicacies as wild raspberries and 
blueberries, tender green (wood-sorrel) 
violet, trillium, plantain, pad-leaf or¬ 
chid and so forth. Roasted nuts, fish 
and even crayfish, makes one think 
twice before going back to lobster. 
Most meals and all evenings were top¬ 
ped off bv a hot drink of wintergreen 
or labrador tea. These, of courseware 
only a few of the more palatable things 
they ate. Thev both lived like kings 
for a week and are looking: forward to 
getting back out at the first possible 
opportunity.” 

—• 


Toronto, Canada 9 April 1961
