The Kayak in Camp 

Hart M. Devenney, M.A. 

It has been our good fortune during 
the past two summers at the Ontario 
Camp Leadership Centre to have been 
introduced to, what was for us anyway, 
a new type of water equipment. Two 
guest instructors from England taught 
us the intricacies of manoeuvering 
Kayaks—and also how to make them. 
The challenge to teen age leaders-in- 
training has resulted in about seven or 
eight new pieces of equipment being 
available to the camp. 

There are a number of advantages to 
the use of the kayak which should com¬ 
mend themselves to the consideration 
of camp directors and program people: 

1. They are inexpensive to make; 
about $30.00 will cover the cost 
of materials. 

2. They are manoeuverable in all 
kinds of water. 

3. They lend themselves to water pro¬ 
grams, not only as a challenge in 
skill, but of interest in boatmanship. 

4. They are light. 

5. They are safe. 

6. They can be made part of most 
craft shop programs as projects for 
senior campers. 

Your first glance at a kayak tells you, 
of course, that here is an unmistakably 
different kind of boat. But it is differ¬ 
ent in such a way as to allow the users 
new kinds of boating pleasures. With it 
you can slip quietly through wooded 
waters or manoeuvre it like nothing 
else through a water slalom course. 
Tricky shallows, submerged logs, rough 
water, allow it to be “knifed through” 
the water in effortless paddling. Be¬ 
cause the paddler is seated below the 
water line rather than on top of it, the 
stability of the kayak is amazing. 

There are plans or kits available on 
the market. Those who are interested 
should write to the author of this article 
for further information. 

—•

8. You are ready to go for more air 
now. Open-scissor your legs to propel 
yourself upward, and begin raising your 
head. Don’t try to raise your head 
until your trunk is vertical. 

9. To keep your head up while inhal¬ 
ing through your mouth, gently sweep 
your palms outward and downward 
smoothly bring your feet together. If 
you get a little water in your mouth, 
spurt it out under water between pursed 
lips. 

The American Red Cross and the 
National Safety Council look on 
Drownproofing with high favour. It is 
taught to hundreds of students at 
Emory University and the University 
of Indiana each year. In Flint, Mich., 
it has been taught to 11,780 persons in 
the last year as part of the school and 
adult-education programs. 

Anyone over the age of four can 
learn the technique with ease. Ad- 


from page 108 

From the very first day, when you 
travel up with them on the train, right 
through the camp days, as you follow 
the forest trails, explore the water-ways 
and get acquainted with them in their 
cabin groups, you will have a wonder¬ 
ful opportunity to give to them the 
things that made camp days such a 
happy adventure for you, and a glorious 
memory of fun and friendliness and 
helpfulness. In other words, you will 
be called upon to give to the campers 
of this summer the very best you have. 

“Give to the world the best you have 
And the best will come back to you!” 

So to you, I present a challenge and 
a warm welcome to the ranks of our 
leaders. May the coming camp season 
be the happiest you have ever known.

Royal Life Saving Society 

LIFE GUARD SERVICE 


“The ability to save life is a glorious 
privilege of a swimmer and many are 
ever ready to risk their own lives in 
order to aid others in danger. This 
ability ought to be cultivated for the 
danger to the rescuer is thereby mini¬ 
mized. Numbers of gallant men have 
been drowned in their vain endeavour 
to rescue because they have not under¬ 
stood the best methods of bringing a 
drowning person to land, or of releasing 
themselves from a grip when clutched. 
Courage and presence of mind are 
essential. It may be argued that if un¬ 
possessed of courage a swimmer would 
never go out to the rescue of another. 
That may be so, but it by no means fol¬ 
lows that presence of mind under diffi¬ 
culties is inherent in the courageous. 
To accomplish a rescue with the least 
possible danger, the two should be 
combined. 5 ’ 

As you read from the above excerpt, 
printed in 1893, the development of 
life saving skills has long received con¬ 
sideration. The Royal Life Saving 
Society has been aware, as have many 
others, that our programs in Canada 
lack a course of training for those per¬ 
sons acting as life guards. With the 
increase in the numbers of people swim¬ 
ming at beaches, camps and pools, this 
deficiency must be corrected as soon as 
possible. 

The Society has been working on 
this project for some time now, and 
should have it in action before the 
summer season opens. 

The program will cover four levels 
of training and examinations, starting 


with the 13 year old, tentatively titled 
Junior Patrol. This provided as a start¬ 
ing point for young swimmers interested 
in being of service under supervision at 
a water area. They are not to be 
thought of as Life Guards or used as 
such. Their interest in this work can 
be stimulated, however, by other water¬ 
front personnel allowing them to assist 
with the equipment, checking and gen¬ 
erally acquiring training and knowledge 
suitable for their age. Their examina¬ 
tion, geared to this level, will require a 
superior knowledge and ability in water 
safety and accident prevention and pro¬ 
cedures in an assisting capacity. 

The 15 year old, tentatively titled 
Life Guard Cadet Corps, is designed 
to enable Bronze Medallion holders, 
interested in advancing their knowledge 
and capabilities in this field, to acquire 
further preparatory training to become 
a life guard. In line with more matur¬ 
ity than that of the 13 year olds, they 
can be given the opportunity to use 
skills they have gained, under adult 
supervision. The pre-requisites for this 
examination necessitate study of first 
aid, artificial respiration and life saving 
skills. Again, superior ability will be 
required to* pass. 

The Society feels that at the age of 
17 a person should be mature enough to 
serve as a life guard. The examination 
qualifies successful candidates for the 
Life Guard Corps. The stiff require¬ 
ments disclose the candidate’s capacity 
to accept the responsibility demanded. 


136 


Canadian Camping 




The examination includes a demonstra¬ 
tion of Life Saving Techniques. This 
shows whether or not the candidate has 
the ability and strength necessary, and 
whether previous training and accom¬ 
plishments have been of a high calibre. 
Through a period of training, preceding 
the tests, candidates will be required to 
learn all phases of life saving. Tn addi¬ 
tion, options covering specific phases of 
interest, such as swimming pools, con¬ 
trolled waterfront, lake or river with 
open area, will be subjected to thorough 
study. 


The Proficiency examination being 
developed will cover the administrative 
and management area of pools and 
waterfront. This will be at a compar¬ 
able level in the Life Guard Service 
to the RLSS highest award, the 
Diploma. 

The Society is fully aware of the 
tremendous undertaking it is assuming. 
Handbooks will have to be printed, 
course and examiners provided. The 
RLSS does feel, however, that it will 
be providing the opportunity to raise 
the standard of employment for this 
responsible job. We will be most inter¬ 
ested in your constructive criticisms. 
We know that amendments, dictated 
by experience, will have to be made, 
but we are endeavouring to keep these 
to a minimum. 

Those in the Society responsible for 
the production of this program have 
given it a great deal of study over a 
lengthy period, but we feel it is of such 
importance that the long term objective 
is justified. They feel confident that 
when the program is put into general 
use it will be the best possible for the 
many and varied situations encountered 
across Canada.

from page \Z6 

from the Spear Tribe, and the Nature 
Lore Director who is a brave, “Running 
Bear” from the Tomahawk Tribe, ap¬ 
pear. The Great Chief tells the braves 
that they have not been allowed to 
marry as there is war between the 
tribes. They now stand on opposite 
sides of the river, looking at each other. 
They mime the song, as four counsellor 
chiefs sing the familiar ballad “Run¬ 
ning Bear and Little White Dove”. 

One of the counsellors had written 
“The Legend of Little Hawkeye”* 2 . 
He now narrates as the campers enact 
the parts. They remember the actions 
well. There are no speaking parts 
which would be difficult for these 
campers. 

One of the chiefs now performs the 
death defying fire dance over and 
around the great fire. 

It is now necessary to bring the little 
braves back to reality and calm, so 
marshmallows are distributed and they 
quietly toast them around their own 
tribal fire. Then all arise and stand in 
a circle and the familiar taps is sung. 

The Moon, high in the heavens, 
smiles down on the braves and their 
chiefs, as they wend their tired but 
happy way up to the hilltop once more. 

*1 —Camp Belwood was a pilot project resi¬ 
dence camp in Canada—begun in 1958. A 
manual is available from O.A.R.C. office, 
77 York St., Suite 300, Toronto, Ontario. 
There are now six camps in Ontario and 
twelve camps throughout Canada. 

The author wishes to thank and give 
credit to Mr. Dan McDade, 1960 Pro¬ 
gramme Director at Camp Belwood. Much 
of his report was used as material for this 
article. Thanks and credit go, too, to the 
wonderful staff who made the whole thing 
possible. 

*2—Available from O.A.R.C. Office.
